extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, courts, and administrative agencies litigating or drafting Section 111(d)/EPA regulations (administrative law practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria for judicial review of EPA's Section 111(d) rulemaking (the Clean Power Plan/ACE Rule), including justiciability (standing/mootness), the definition and limits of the 'best system of emission reduction' (BSER), and application of the major questions/clear-statement principles in administrative-rule interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article III standing at the appellate stage
rubrics_metrics.description: A litigant seeking appellate review must show an injury 'fairly traceable to the judgment below' and that a 'favorable ruling' would redress that injury; Article III standing must persist throughout all stages of litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'In considering a litigant’s standing to appeal, the question is whether it has experienced an injury “fairly traceable to the judgment below.” … If so, and a “favorable ruling” from the appellate court “would redress [that] injury,” then the appellant has a cognizable Article III stake.' (citing Food Marketing Institute v. Argus Leader Media). Applies equally to appellants as to plaintiffs in trial courts. Example: State petitioners are injured because the D.C. Circuit's judgment purported to bring the Clean Power Plan back into legal effect, imposing more stringent regulation within their borders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between standing and mootness; burden on respondent for mootness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an intervening circumstance has deprived the plaintiff of a personal stake is a mootness question (not standing), and the Government bears the burden of establishing that a once-live case has become moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'The distinction matters because the Government, not petitioners, bears the burden to establish that a once‑live case has become moot.' Voluntary cessation by a defendant does not moot a case unless it is 'absolutely clear that the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.' (citing Friends of the Earth and Parents Involved). A lower court's stay of mandate does not, by itself, extinguish the controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine / clear congressional authorization for extraordinary agency assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency claims power over matters of vast economic and political significance (a 'major question'), courts expect Congress to have spoken clearly; an agency must point to 'clear congressional authorization' for the power it claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'Under that doctrine, courts “expect Congress to speak clearly if it wishes to assign to an agency decisions of vast economic and political significance.”' The agency must show more than a merely plausible textual basis; extraordinary cases call for hesitation and require clear statement evidence (citing Brown & Williamson, Utility Air, King v. Burwell, etc.). The label 'major questions doctrine' collects prior precedents addressing common threads (history, breadth, significance, novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors indicating a 'major questions' case
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances that transform an interpretation into a major-questions situation include the history and breadth of asserted authority, the economic and political significance of the action, novelty of the agency's claim (an 'unheralded' power), and whether Congress has repeatedly declined to enact similar measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Courts consider whether the claimed power represents a 'transformative expansion' of regulatory authority, is located in a peripheral or ancillary provision, has been rarely used, and would authorize wholesale restructuring of an industry. Examples from precedent: FDA/tobacco regulation (Brown & Williamson), CDC eviction moratorium (Alabama Assn. of Realtors), EPA greenhouse-gas permitting (Utility Air).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and centrality of BSER under 42 U.S.C. §7411(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must determine the 'best system of emission reduction' (BSER) that has 'been adequately demonstrated,' and then quantify 'the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application' of that system; BSER is the central determination in formulating emission guidelines under Section 111.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote statutory language and EPA practice: 'The Agency then quantifies “the degree of emission limitation achievable” if that best system were applied to the covered source.' In practice, this involves identifying a system (or combination of controls/measures) that is adequately demonstrated and then translating it into operational emissions limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/typical understanding of Section 111 as technology-based (BDT) standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111 historically has been interpreted as authorizing technology-based standards that focus on improving emissions performance of individual sources—'best demonstrated technology' or similar 'level of control' applied at the source (building, structure, facility, or installation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's longstanding practice (and early rulemaking language) described Section 111 as intending 'a technology-based approach' (e.g., 'best adequately demonstrated control technology'). Examples: efficiency improvements, fuel-switching, add-on controls; the rulemaking record repeatedly treated Section 111 standards as BDT/technology-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: BSER must have potential application to an individual source (not grid-wide generation shifting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures that make up the BSER must be capable of being put into operation 'at a building, structure, facility, or installation'—i.e., have potential application to an individual source; grid-wide generation shifting is not an LSER measure of that kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: EPA's 2019 interpretation: Section 111 'limit[s] the BSER to those systems that can be put into operation at a building, structure, facility, or installation.' The Court contrasts prior at-source controls (installable devices like wet scrubbers) with the Clean Power Plan's generation-shifting limits, noting 'there is no control a coal plant operator can deploy to attain the emissions limits established by the Clean Power Plan.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory factors to consider when choosing BSER and translating it into stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: In selecting BSER and determining the degree of emission limitation achievable, the agency must take into account statutory factors including 'cost,' 'nonair quality health and environmental impact,' and 'energy requirements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote statute: 42 U. S. C. §7411(a)(1). The agency may use modeling to choose from a 'wide range of potential stringencies' but should base limits on assessments of feasibility, costs, impacts, and reliability (e.g., projections about share of coal generation, grid reliability, energy prices). The Court notes agency modeling used to justify a 'reasonable' generation shift (e.g., coal from 38% to 27% by 2030).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness and limits on agency choice of stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an agency can choose among a wide range of potential stringencies for BSER, it must set a level that is 'reasonable'—taking into account feasibility, undue costs, and reliability concerns—and not an unbounded preference that effects wholesale sectoral restructuring absent clear congressional authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: EPA modeled how much more electricity cleaner sources could supply 'without causing undue cost increases or reducing the overall power supply' and settled on what it regarded as a 'reasonable' amount of generation shifting. The Court cautions that allowing the agency to resolve such tradeoffs effectively assigns major national energy-policy decisions to the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of historical practice and lack of prior assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: A consistent history of agency practice that never asserted the claimed power (and the absence of reliance on such authority in the statute's history) weighs against interpreting a statutory provision to confer that power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: The Court cites the unbroken list of prior Section 111 rules that set caps based on controls installable on sources and notes that 'want of assertion of power by those who presumably would be alert to exercise it, is equally significant' (FTC v. Bunte Brothers). A single controversial but unlitigated Mercury Rule does not overcome the broader historical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive canon: courts presume Congress intends to make major policy decisions itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts presume that Congress does not delegate major social and economic policy decisions to agencies through vague or modest statutory language; extraordinary or 'radical' changes to a statutory scheme are unlikely to rest on oblique language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote/paraphrase: 'We presume that “Congress intends to make major policy decisions itself, not leave those decisions to agencies.”' Cases cited include Brown & Williamson, MCI, Whitman. This functions as a presumption requiring clearer statutory evidence before upholding agency actions that effect sweeping changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of precedent/examples of major-questions analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior cases (Brown & Williamson, Utility Air, Gonzales v. Oregon, Alabama Assn. of Realtors, NFIB/OSHA) show how major-questions concerns were applied: court rejected expansive agency claims despite colorable textual bases when consequences were transformative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Use these precedents as analogues to determine whether an agency's claimed authority is 'unheralded' or would grant 'unprecedented' regulatory power over significant portions of the economy; the existence of similar past nonuse or congressional inaction is telling.
